name: Hindu Texts
fw: CCSS RL/RI/RH / C3 / IL SS 9–12 / Teaching About Religion
fwnote: The course reads a tradition's texts as literature and as historical sources in a public school, so it cites the reading standards for the band (RL, RI, RH, WHST), C3 history for 6–8, Illinois SS.H 9–12, and one of the six principles in "A Teacher's Guide to Religion in the Public Schools" (First Amendment Center) that the AAR 2010 Guidelines build on; alignment is the course author's judgment, not a certification or an endorsement by any of these bodies.

1.bq: What can a story about a promise and helpers teach us?
std: RL.K.2
With prompting and support, retell familiar stories with their key details.
Retell stories with key details and show you understand their central message or lesson.
Describe the characters, settings and major events of a story using key details.
Teaching About Religion · academic not devotional
Study religion as an academic subject that describes beliefs and practices without leading worship.
1.write: Draw and tell. Pick one helper from the Ramayana: Lakshmana, Hanuman or the little squirrel. Draw how they helped. Tell a grown-up what the story says they did.
rooms: Daily Practice — Hindu texts, grades K–2

ch.t: Rama, Sita and the Golden Deer
ch.bq: Why do people keep a promise when it is hard?
ch.talk: Sita saw something beautiful and wanted it. Have you ever wanted something you saw?

l.look: Who tells you stories at home? What is your favorite one?
Point to Rama. Point to Sita. How can you tell who is who?
Rama is not angry. Why do you think he says yes?
Count them. How many people went to the forest?

l.t: A Deer That Is a Trick
l.look: What clue tells you this deer is not a real deer?
Why is dropping the jewels a smart idea?

ch.t: Hanuman the Brave Helper
ch.bq: How can every helper, big or small, make a difference?
ch.talk: The squirrel was very small. Was its help important? Why?

l.look: Hanuman's hands are together. What might that show about him?
How many ways did the groups go?
How do you think Sita felt when she saw the ring?
How does it feel when someone thanks you for helping?
Why do you think families love to tell this story?
Why do you think the people lit so many lamps?
Why might a family light lamps by the door?

2.t: Krishna, Ganesha and the Stories Families Tell
2.bq: What do the stories families tell help children learn?
std: Retell stories with key details and show you understand their central message or lesson.
Retell stories, fables and folktales from different cultures and state the lesson or message they teach.
Teaching About Religion · aware not accepting
Build students' understanding of religions without pressing them to accept any one.
2.write: Draw and tell. Pick one story: Krishna and the hill, or Ganesha and the race. Draw the most important part. Tell a grown-up what happens and what families say it teaches.
rooms: Daily Practice — Hindu texts, grades K–2

ch.t: Krishna and the Mountain
ch.bq: How can we share and keep others safe?
ch.talk: Krishna kept everyone safe. Who keeps you safe when it storms?

l.t: A Boy in a Cowherd Village
l.look: What sounds might you hear in this village?
Krishna shares the butter. Who does he share it with?
Tell about a time you shared something. How did it feel?
What do you do to stay safe in a storm?
How long does Krishna hold up the hill?
Why do you think the family waits until midnight?
How many Krishna stories did you learn?

ch.t: Ganesha and the Race Around the World
ch.bq: How can thinking in a new way help us?
ch.talk: Ganesha found a new way to win. Why did his parents like his answer?

l.look: What do you notice first about Ganesha?
Why might this family think of Ganesha first in a new home?
Why do you think a big Ganesha rides a small mouse?
Who do you think will be faster? Why?
What does Ganesha mean when he says his parents are his world?
Why do families set out foods they say Ganesha loves?
How is the girl like Ganesha in the race?

3.bq: How do festivals and stories help people be kind?
std: D2.Geo.6.K-2
Name some of the cultural and environmental features of particular places.
Retell stories, fables and folktales from different cultures and state the lesson or message they teach.
NCSS 1 · Culture
How people create, learn, share and adapt culture, and how cultures compare.
Teaching About Religion · study not practice
Teach about religious practices without having students take part in them.
3.write: Draw and tell. Pick Diwali or Holi. Draw one thing families do. Tell a grown-up what they do and what many families say it means.
rooms: Daily Practice — Hindu texts, grades K–2

ch.t: Diwali: The Festival of Lights
ch.bq: Why do so many families light lamps at Diwali?
ch.talk: Priya made something beautiful to welcome people. How does your family get ready for a special day?

l.look: Why might a festival last more than one day?
How does the house look different with all the lamps?
Can two families keep the same festival with different stories? How?
What flower goes with Lakshmi?
How many faiths on this list light lamps at Diwali?
What shapes can you see in a rangoli? Name two.
Which step would you like to help with? Why?
What can one small light do in a dark room?

ch.t: Holi, Namaste and Helping Others
ch.bq: How can we be kind to people and to every living thing?
ch.talk: Arjun and Meera made up. What helps you make up with a friend?

l.look: Name three colors you see in this picture.
Why is a festival a good time to make up?
How does Prahlada act when his father is angry?
Why do families tell a story around the fire?
What are different ways people say hello? Name two.
What does this old book say is the highest duty?
Which way to help could you do this week?

4.bq: How have Hindus kept a great library of sacred texts alive for thousands of years?
std: Determine the main idea of a text, explain how details support it, and summarize.
Teaching About Religion · expose not impose
Introduce a range of religious views without imposing any particular one.
4.write: Is it better to think of Hindu scripture as one book or as a library? Use two texts from this unit, such as the Rig Veda, Chandogya Upanishad 6.13 or Bhagavad Gita 2.47. Say which group each belongs to and how Hindus have used it.
rooms: World Religions unit 6 — Traditions of India and East Asia

ch.t: Heard and Remembered: Shruti and Smriti
ch.bq: How do Hindus sort their many sacred texts?
ch.talk: Why might a religion have a whole library instead of one book?

l.look: Which side of the shelf would the Ramayana go on? How do you know?

l.t: The Names Hindu and Sanatana Dharma
l.look: What does each name tell you about the tradition?
Which group honors Shiva above all?
How is a traditional view different from a scholar's date?
How many hymns are in the Rig Veda?
Who is the teacher here, and who is the student?
Which two texts are shruti? How did you decide?
About how many times longer is the Mahabharata?
What does Krishna say about rewards?
Why do you think the Puranas are so loved by families?

ch.t: Sanskrit, Gurus and Memory
ch.bq: How did the Hindu texts travel across thousands of years?
ch.talk: Why would a teacher make students chant the words in so many patterns?

l.look: Why do you think these words look so alike?
Which of these words have you heard before?
How can one word look different but sound the same?
What could you do to keep a message from changing?
How would these patterns help you catch a mistake?
How can people protect a treasure that cannot be touched?
How does the salt help the student understand?
Why would scribes need to copy these books again and again?
Which telling is the newest? Which is the oldest?
How is this like the old way of learning? How is it different?

5.bq: What does the Ramayana teach about doing what is right, and why do people tell it in so many ways?
std: Recount fables, folktales and myths from diverse cultures and explain the central message.
Describe a character's traits, motives and feelings and how the character's actions move the events.
Determine a theme from how characters respond to challenges, and summarize the text.
Teaching About Religion · educate not promote or denigrate
Present every tradition fairly, neither advancing nor disparaging religion.
5.write: Which character in the Ramayana best shows dharma? Choose one: Rama, Bharata, Lakshmana or Sita. Use two scenes from the unit, naming the kanda (for example, Ayodhya Kanda or Sundara Kanda). Explain what the poem says and how Hindus have read it.
rooms: World Religions unit 6 — Traditions of India and East Asia

ch.t: Valmiki's Poem: From Ayodhya to the Forest
ch.bq: What does it mean to do what is right for your role?
ch.talk: Bharata could have been king. Why do you think he put the sandals on the throne instead?

s.t: The First Poet and His Poem

l.look: What feeling does the poem say started Valmiki's poetry?
In which book does the battle happen?
How can you report both answers fairly in one sentence?
Which queen had twins?
What two good things are pulling against each other for the king?
Why do you think the poem shows Rama as calm, not angry?
What do the sandals stand for in this part of the story?
How is this life different from life in a palace?
Pick one person. What role is that person living up to?
Why might a poet retell a story that people already know?

ch.t: Lanka, Return and the Meaning of Dharma
ch.bq: Why do people keep retelling the Ramayana, and why do their tellings differ?
ch.talk: Why might people want to watch the same story every year?

l.look: What does Sita's answer show about her?
What qualities of Hanuman might a family want to remember each day?
Was Vibhishana's choice hard? Why?
What does this scene show about Hanuman's loyalty?
How does the story connect to what families do at Diwali?
Pick two qualities of a good leader. Explain why they matter.
How can readers who love the same story still disagree about it?
How does the feeling of the story change when you switch perspective?
Which country calls its telling the Ramakien?
Why might a play end on this moment?

6.bq: What does the Mahabharata teach about doing what is right when every choice is hard?
std: Work out a story's theme from its details and summarize the text.
Describe a character, setting or event in depth, drawing on specific details in the text.
Teaching About Religion · inform not conform
Inform students about beliefs without asking them to conform to any.
6.write: Was Arjuna right to be afraid to fight? Use Bhagavad Gita 1.28–32 (Arjuna's sorrow) and 2.47 (Krishna's answer), in Telang's translation (1882). Explain what the Gita says, and how two readers, such as a reader who sees a real war and Gandhi, have read it.
rooms: World Religions unit 6 — Traditions of India and East Asia

ch.t: Two Families, One Kingdom
ch.bq: How do you decide what is right when everyone has a reason?
ch.talk: Why do you think no one stopped the game? What might you have done?

l.look: About how many times longer is the Mahabharata than the Ramayana?
What does this legend suggest about how hard some parts of the Mahabharata are?
Why might a story grow longer each time it is told?
Which brother is the best archer? Which is the eldest?
Why might a story show a rival as partly good?
Why is it brave to ask a hard question in front of powerful people?
Why is Draupadi's question so hard for the elders to answer?
How many years in all are the Pandavas away?
What might have happened if Duryodhana had said yes?
Which loyalty would you choose, and why? Can you explain the other side too?

ch.t: Arjuna's Question and Stories Inside the Story
ch.bq: What should you do when your duty feels too hard?
ch.talk: Savitri did not fight Death. How did she win?

l.look: What number shows up twice in this table?
Why does Arjuna not want to win?
Why might a teacher be shown as a driver in this story?

l.t: Do Your Duty, Not for the Reward
l.look: Put this verse in your own words. What does it mean for a student?

l.t: The Self That Does Not Die
l.look: What does the comparison to clothes help a reader picture?

l.t: Many Ways to Read the Gita
l.look: How can the same scene be read in two such different ways?
What does Savitri's answer show about her?
How did Savitri use Yama's own promise to win?
Why is this story a good one to tell Yudhishthira right now?
Why might a very long story say it contains everything?

7.bq: How do Hindu ideas and festivals help families live out the stories of their texts?
std: Determine the main idea of a text, explain how details support it, and summarize.
NCSS 1 · Culture
How people create, learn, share and adapt culture, and how cultures compare.
Teaching About Religion · study not practice
Teach about religious practices without having students take part in them.
7.write: Pick one Hindu festival from this unit. Explain what story it remembers and which idea it connects to (dharma, karma or bhakti). Cite the text, such as the Ramayana or the Bhagavata Purana, and one Gita verse if it fits.

ch.t: Dharma, Karma, Samsara, Moksha
ch.bq: What big ideas do Hindu texts teach about how to live, and how do stories help people remember them?
ch.talk: Why do you think Dada used a seed to explain karma? What other picture could help someone understand an idea like this?

l.t: Dharma: The Right Way to Live
l.look: Why might dharma look different for a student, a father and a king? What is one duty you have at school?
What does Krishna tell Arjuna to care about: the work or the prize? Say it in your own words.
Which aim do the texts say should guide the other three?
What is compared to clothes in this verse? What is compared to the person wearing them?
How are these two pictures of moksha alike? How are they different?

l.t: Karma in a Story You Know
l.look: What action did Hanuman take? What result came from it? How might a Hindu storyteller use this to teach karma?
What does this verse say about names? How do many Hindus use it to explain many forms?
Which chapter of the Gita is known for teaching about devotion?
Match each picture to one idea: dharma, karma, samsara or moksha. Explain one match.

ch.t: A Year of Festivals and a Temple Near Chicago
ch.bq: How do Hindu festivals and worship keep the stories of the texts alive for families today?
ch.talk: The students took off their shoes and used quiet voices. Why do you think visitors show respect in these ways at a place of worship?

s.t: A Calendar of Moon and Sun

l.look: About how many days short are 12 moon months compared with a sun year? Why might calendars add an extra month?
Why might one festival hold two different stories? What do both families share?
Why do you think the pot overflowing is a happy sign at a harvest festival?
What might the lamps stand for, according to many Hindus? Use the words light and darkness.
What did Prahlad keep doing? How does the Holi bonfire help people remember his story?
Which comes right after the nine nights? What story do many people remember on that day?
Why might a family celebrate at midnight on Janmashtami?
Which offering becomes prasad after worship?
What does darshan mean? Why might the mother want her toddler to see the murti?
Write three things you would do to show respect during the visit. Why does each one matter?

8.bq: What are the Vedas, and how have Hindus kept them alive and used them for over three thousand years?
std: Work out figurative and connotative meanings and the effect of repetition and sound in poetry.
Determine the meaning of words and phrases in a text, including terms specific to history and society.
Teaching About Religion · academic not devotional
Study religion as an academic subject that describes beliefs and practices without leading worship.
8.write: Why have the Vedas lasted so long? Cite two or three passages from this unit, such as Rig Veda 1.1.1, 3.62.10 or 10.129.7 (Griffith, 1896), and explain what they say and how Hindus have used and kept them.
rooms: How to read a sacred text — the room

ch.t: Hymns of the Rig Veda
ch.bq: What do the hymns of the Rig Veda praise and ask, and why have Hindus kept them alive for so long?
ch.talk: The priest learned the hymns by listening, not reading. What would it take to keep a long text perfectly in memory for hundreds of years?

l.look: About how many verses does each hymn have, on average? Round your answer.

l.t: Hymns as Poems and Ritual Words
l.look: How is the hymn being used differently in each setting? What stays the same?
What titles does this verse give Agni? Which words sound old-fashioned to you?
Which two gods receive the most hymns? What might that tell you about what mattered to the poets?
What does Vritra hold back? Why might people in a hot, dry land tell this story?
What does the hymn notice about the dawn and about people? How do you feel reading it?
What does the speaker hope Savitar will do? Why might someone say this at sunrise?
What question does this verse leave open? Why might a sacred text end a creation hymn with a question?
What does each reader think about the verse? How could you describe these views fairly without judging all Hindus?
About how many years passed between the end of the Rig Veda and Griffith's translation?

ch.t: Four Vedas, Ritual and an Unbroken Voice
ch.bq: How were the four Vedas organized, used and passed down, and who has been allowed to learn them?
ch.talk: The teacher says the patterns will catch mistakes. How is this like the ways you check your own work in math or spelling?
ch.story: Eleven Ways to Say One Verse

l.look: Match each person with the Veda that best fits: Rig, Sama, Yajur or Atharva. Explain one match.
Which layer explains rituals? Which layer asks about the self?
Sort these into shruti and smriti. Which one would many Hindus know best, and why?
How is this home havan like the old Vedic yajna? How is it different?

l.t: The Vedas at Weddings and Life Rites
l.look: Which of these rites begins formal learning? Which comes last?
How is this offering different from a large Vedic yajna? What matters most, according to this verse?
Do you agree with the teacher? What are the strengths of memory and of writing?
Why would saying a word more times help catch mistakes?
What does this passage show about women and learning in the Upanishads?
Why might protecting a chant be harder than protecting a building? What helps keep it alive?

9.bq: What do the Upanishads teach about the self and reality, and why do they teach it through questions?
std: Determine a source's central ideas and give an accurate summary free of prior opinions.
Determine a theme, analyze how it develops through characters, setting and plot, and summarize objectively.
Teaching About Religion · aware not accepting
Build students' understanding of religions without pressing them to accept any one.
9.write: What does 'That art thou' mean? Cite Chandogya 6.8.7 and one other passage (Müller, SBE 1 or 15). Explain what the text says and how Shankara and Ramanuja or Madhva read it.
rooms: World Religions unit 11 — South and East Asian Traditions

ch.t: Atman and Brahman: Teachers in the Forest
ch.bq: What do the Upanishads teach about the self and ultimate reality, and how have Hindu schools read those teachings differently?
ch.talk: Why do you think Uddalaka used salt and water instead of just telling his son the answer?

l.look: Why might scholars focus on about a dozen out of 108?

l.t: Vedanta: The End of the Veda
l.look: About how many years separate Shankara and Madhva?
How do these English versions of the same Sanskrit words differ? Why might the wording change what a reader thinks the passage means?
What does this passage say about the self and the body? Which verse in the Gita says something similar?
What is the teacher trying to show? Why might some ideas be easier to describe by what they are not?
What does Uddalaka say all that exists has its self in? What does he say Svetaketu is?
In this picture, what stands for the world, what for Brahman, and what for knowledge?
How do these three pictures differ? Which words in each show what the school believes about the self?
What three pairs of opposites does the prayer name? Why might people from many schools use it?
How many years passed between the Persian translation and Vivekananda's Chicago speech?

ch.t: Stories of the Upanishads
ch.bq: Why do the Upanishads teach through questions and conversations, and what do their stories show about learning?
ch.talk: Why do you think Nachiketa turns down gold and kingdoms? What does his choice say about him?

l.look: Why do you think the hardest question is the last wish?
Give an example from school life of the good and the pleasant pulling in different directions.
What happens to the chariot if the horses run wild? What does that stand for?
What is Uddalaka teaching with the seed? How is it like the salt lesson?
Why does the teacher accept Satyakama? What does he value most?
What do these openings have in common? What does that suggest about how these texts see learning?
What is Gargi doing with her questions? Why might a teacher say, 'Do not ask too far'?
What does Maitreyi choose instead of wealth? How is her choice like Nachiketa's?
Which of these questioners are young? Which are women? What does the list show?

10.bq: How did epics, Puranas and poet-saints carry Hindu teaching to people of every language and background?
std: Describe how a text presents information, such as in order, by comparison or by cause.
Determine a theme, analyze how it develops through characters, setting and plot, and summarize objectively.
Teaching About Religion · expose not impose
Introduce a range of religious views without imposing any particular one.
10.write: How do Hindu epics teach dharma through story? Cite two or three passages, such as the dice game (Mahabharata, Sabha Parva), Savitri (Vana Parva) or Valmiki's first verse (Bala Kanda), naming Ganguli or Griffith. Explain what happens and how readers have understood it.

ch.t: Itihasa: Epic as Story and Teaching
ch.bq: How do the Ramayana and Mahabharata tell stories and teach dharma at the same time?
ch.talk: Why might a storyteller put stories inside other stories? What does it do for the listener?

l.look: About how many times longer than the Ramayana is the Mahabharata?
What is each person basing their view on? How could you report both views fairly?
What feeling leads to the first verse? Why might tradition link poetry with grief?
Why might a storyteller repeat one number so often?
Put these events in order and name the kanda where each happens.
How does Savitri win? Compare her with Nachiketa, who also met Yama.
Why is Draupadi's question so hard? What does the silence of the elders show?
Is Karna's loyalty a strength, a flaw, or both? What might the epic be teaching?
How many years did Ganguli's Mahabharata take to publish?
How might a reader of each version feel differently about Rama? Why do you think new versions appeared?

ch.t: Puranas and the Bhakti Poets
ch.bq: How did the Puranas and the bhakti poets bring Hindu devotion into everyday languages and lives?
ch.talk: Why do you think Mirabai's songs spread so widely, even though she left the palace behind?

l.look: Which text is much shorter? Why might a short text be easier to recite?

l.t: The Bhagavata and the Devi Mahatmya
l.look: What does this story show about Krishna, as his devotees see him? Why might Indra's role matter?
Which avatars in this list are animals? Which are human heroes?
Why might a poet choose a human relationship to describe devotion? Which relationship shows the most closeness to you?
How many more Nayanars are there than Alvars?
What is the poet saying about devotion and the rules of the temple? Why might his song spread?

s.t: Bhakti in the North and West

l.look: Whom does Mira call her only one? What is she willing to give up?
What does this story say about Kabir's place between traditions? Why might people tell it?
About how many centuries passed between the Tamil poet-saints and Tukaram?

11.bq: How have Hindu texts changed and traveled through history, and how do we tell that history fairly?
std: Analyze how events and developments connect within their wider historical setting.
Detect gaps and limits in the historical record by comparing different kinds of sources.
Analyze how a modern work draws on themes, patterns or character types from traditional stories or religious works.
Teaching About Religion · educate not promote or denigrate
Present every tradition fairly, neither advancing nor disparaging religion.
11.write: How has one Hindu text changed as it traveled? Pick the Gita or the Ramayana. Cite two or three moments from the unit, such as Gita 4.11 in Vivekananda's 1893 address, Gandhi's reading via Arnold's The Song Celestial (1885), or Angkor Wat's carvings, and explain how each reader or place used it.
rooms: World Religions unit 11 — South and East Asian Traditions

ch.t: From the Indus to the Guptas
ch.bq: How did Hindu texts and traditions take shape over thousands of years, and how do scholars and Hindus tell that history?
ch.talk: Why is it so hard to know what the seal means? What would help scholars answer the question?

l.look: About how many years did the big Indus cities last?
Sort each claim into known, inferred or unknown. Explain one choice.
What can a historian learn from what a hymn mentions and does not mention? What are the limits?
Which came first by these estimates, the oldest Upanishads or the Buddha?
What is each clock measuring? Why might both appear in a Hindu family's home?
Describe each response in one sentence. Why might Hindus disagree about one old text?
About how long did Gupta rule last?
How many years passed between the Brihadishvara temple and India's independence?
Write one fair sentence that names both views about the Rig Veda's age.

ch.t: Texts on the Move: Asia, Chicago and Today
ch.bq: How have Hindu texts traveled beyond India, and what have new readers made of them?
ch.talk: Why do you think Vivekananda's greeting moved the audience so much? What did it say about how he saw them?

l.look: Which epic and which character might this carving show? Why would a king carve these stories on a temple?
Why might Hindu traditions be strong on one island but small in the country overall?
Why might he bring that book? What could it mean to him and his family far from home?
What does Thoreau compare reading the Gita to? What does that suggest about how he felt?
What feeling does Vivekananda express? Why might he begin by thanking the audience?
What does each reader think the battle means? What in the Gita might support each reading?
About what share of U.S. adults are Hindu? How does that compare with other groups?
How might their pictures of Rama and Sita differ? What is gained and lost when one version becomes widely known?
How is each person using the Gita? Which uses might some Hindus welcome, and which might worry them? Why?

12.bq: What does the Gita teach about action and duty, and why do its readers disagree about what that means?
std: Determine a theme and analyze in detail how specific details develop and shape it.
Analyze how specific word choices, including figurative language, build meaning and tone.
Analyze a point of view or cultural experience in a work of world literature from outside the United States.
Teaching About Religion · academic not devotional
Study religion as an academic subject that describes beliefs and practices without leading worship.
12.write: Does the Gita tell Arjuna to set aside his conscience or to act from a steadier one? Cite two or three verses from Gita 1–6 or 18.63 (chapter and verse, with the translation), explain what each says, and describe how at least two readers (for example Gandhi and Tilak) have understood them.
rooms: World Religions unit 18 — Hinduism: Dharma, Karma and the Gita

ch.t: Arjuna's Despair and Krishna's Answer
ch.bq: What does Krishna say to a person who cannot bring himself to act, and how have readers understood his answer?
ch.talk: Arjuna refuses to act because he loves his family. Is his refusal weakness, wisdom, or something else? What would you need to know to decide?

l.look: The Gita is a small part of a very large epic. Why might a short dialogue be placed at the moment just before battle?
Why might the poet list family roles instead of saying "the enemy army"? What does the list make a reader feel?
What is Arjuna weighing against what? Put his reasoning into one sentence of your own.
Why might the Gita have Arjuna ask to be taught before Krishna begins? How does that change the kind of talk that follows?
Find the words in this verse that deny time (born, die, again). Why might this verse be read at funerals?
What in the picture stays the same, and what changes? What does the image suggest about how Arjuna should see death?

l.t: Your Right Is to the Work
l.look: Name one job, sport or school task where focusing on the work instead of the grade might change how you do it.
What does a tortoise do when it is in danger? What might it mean for a person to "draw in" the senses, and when might that help?
At which step do you think it would be easiest to stop the chain? Give a reason.
If you were writing a close-reading essay, which would you quote to show exactly what the Sanskrit says? Which might you quote to show how the Gita was felt by English readers?

l.t: An Outer War or an Inner One
l.look: Find one line in Gita 1 or 2 that each reader could use to support their view. Can both readings be held together?

ch.t: Action Without Clinging
ch.bq: Can a person do their work fully while letting go of what they will get from it?
ch.talk: What part of a job is in a worker's control, and what part is not? How might that difference change how a person feels after a hard day?

l.look: List three actions you do without choosing them. How does this verse change the question "Should I act?"
Why might the Gita choose a king, not a hermit, as its example? What does that suggest about ordinary jobs?
What would each reading tell a student who wants a career different from her parents'? Describe each fairly.
Who is speaking, and to whom? What three purposes does the speaker name?
Describe a person who is busy on the outside but calm inside, and a person who is still on the outside but restless inside. Which fits each half of the verse?
What is the fuel, and what is the fire, in this image? Why might the poet choose fire rather than water?

l.t: A Seat, Neither High nor Low
l.look: Why do you think the text gives such specific physical details? What does it suggest about how body and mind are related in the Gita?

l.t: The Lamp and the Restless Mind
l.look: Both images use air. How does the second image answer the first? What does Krishna's reply in 6.35 add?
These four works came out within about fifty years. What was happening in India during those years that might explain the interest?
How does 18.63 affect the debate about duty and conscience? Build one argument on each side using this verse.

13.bq: How do the Gita and the Upanishads teach about the self, God and devotion, and why do their readers understand them differently?
std: Analyze how specific word choices, including figurative language, build meaning and tone.
Analyze a point of view or cultural experience in a work of world literature from outside the United States.
Determine a source's central ideas and give an accurate summary of how key ideas develop.
Teaching About Religion · study not practice
Teach about religious practices without having students take part in them.
13.write: Do the Gita and the Upanishads picture the path to the highest goal in the same way? Cite two or three passages (for example Gita 9.26 or 18.66, Katha 1.3.3, Chandogya 6.13; give the translation), explain what each says, and describe how at least two schools of readers have understood them.
rooms: World Religions unit 18 — Hinduism: Dharma, Karma and the Gita

ch.t: Devotion and the Universal Form
ch.bq: How does the Gita join love and awe, and how have its different readers understood its final teaching?
ch.talk: Arjuna wants to see the whole truth, and then cannot bear it. Why might the poem show both his wish and his fear?

s.t: A Leaf, a Flower, a Fruit

l.look: The wind moves; space does not. What does the image suggest about the relation between beings and the one who speaks? Who is speaking?
What four offerings are named? Why might the text choose such simple things?
What does this verse open up? What does it take for granted about its society? Write one sentence for each.
Sanjaya uses a comparison because words fail. What does comparing to "a thousand suns" tell us about what Arjuna saw?
Why might the scientist have thought of this verse? How is his situation like Arjuna's, and how is it different?
Why does Arjuna name three human relationships right after the terrifying vision? What does this suggest about how the Gita pictures devotion?

s.t: The Devotee and the Final Word

l.look: Why might a poem repeat "dear to me" several times? What does repetition do for a listener?
What might "giving up all duties" mean, given that Arjuna goes on to fight? Name two readings.
Pick one verse from this chapter that each reader might cite. How does each reader's map change the meaning of that verse?
The epic uses the number 18 again and again. Why might storytellers repeat a number like this?

ch.t: Katha, Chandogya and Isha: "That Art Thou"
ch.bq: How do the Upanishads use questions, teachers and simple images to teach about the self and Brahman?
ch.talk: The father could have simply told his son the answer. Why might he have asked him to break open the seed instead?

l.t: Texts at the End of the Veda
l.look: Why would the layer that asks the deepest questions come last? What might have changed over time?
Answer the three questions for the salt scene, even before you read it in full. What do you predict the teacher wants to show?
How do the wishes move from near to far? Why might the Upanishad save the deepest question for last?
Describe a choice a student might face between the good and the pleasant. Why does Yama test Nachiketa before teaching him?
Match each part of the chariot to a part of the person. Which part does the steering, and which part only rides?
Who speaks, and to whom? What does "it" refer to? Why might a teacher repeat this line at the end of each lesson?
Count the steps in this dialogue. Why does the teacher ask the student to break the seed himself?
What does each image teach that the other does not? Why might a teacher use both?
How can someone enjoy something by letting go of it? Give one example from ordinary life.
What words are nearly the same? What is different about the setting of each passage?

14.bq: How do ancient hymns and epic dilemmas pose hard questions, and how have different readers answered them?
std: Analyze how complex characters with conflicting motives develop, interact and advance the theme.
Analyze how specific word choices, including figurative language, build meaning and tone.
Teaching About Religion · inform not conform
Inform students about beliefs without asking them to conform to any.
14.write: Do the texts in this unit give clear answers to hard questions, or do they leave the questions open? Cite two or three passages (for example Rig Veda 10.129.7 in Griffith, Draupadi's question in the Sabha Parva, Sita's return in the Uttara Kanda), explain what each says, and describe how different readers have responded.

ch.t: The Hymn of Creation and the Purusha Hymn
ch.bq: What happens when two ancient hymns from the same book, one full of questions and one describing a social order, are read closely and side by side?
ch.talk: Why might a sacred hymn end with a question instead of an answer? What might that tell you about the people who composed and kept it?

l.look: The two hymns you will study are both in Book 10. What does their size tell you about how much of the whole they are?
What is the same in both? What does Griffith's word order do to the sound of the line?
The poet describes the beginning using only what was not there. Why might someone describe a beginning this way?

l.t: Desire and the Seed of Mind
l.look: Why might poets look into their own hearts to understand the beginning of the world? What does this say about how they saw themselves?
Find the two places where the verse leaves an "or" open. How would the verse feel if the last four words were removed?
What does the number "thousand" suggest here? How is this opening different from the opening of 10.129?
The verse names the parts from head to foot. What does that order suggest? What does the image of one body suggest?

l.t: How the Verse Was Used, and Answered
l.look: What does each response keep, and what does each reject? Describe each position in words its holder would accept.
Describe the tone of each hymn in two words. What might explain why one collection keeps both?
Can both settings be real and important at once? How should a writer describe both fairly?

ch.t: Dharma Dilemmas: Dice, the Yaksha and Sita's Trial
ch.bq: When the epics show good people facing hard choices, what do they teach about dharma, and why do readers disagree?
ch.talk: Bhishma says dharma is subtle and stays silent. Is silence a way of keeping dharma, or of failing it? What would you need to know to decide?

l.look: Why does it matter that he lost himself before he staked Draupadi? This order is the basis of her question.
Bhishma gives two rules that point in opposite directions. What are they? Why might the poet show a wise elder stuck between them?
Find a detail in the scene that supports each reader. Is there a detail that none of them explains?
What might the story be saying about the difference between Yudhishthira and his brothers? Think about the dice game too.
Why does Yudhishthira call this a wonder rather than a mistake? What is he asking the listener to notice?
What does this choice show about how Yudhishthira understands dharma? Do you think it was the right choice? Give a reason from the story.
Why might Karna feel bound to Duryodhana for life? Was Duryodhana's act kindness, strategy, or both?
State the strongest reason for each choice. Which reason do you find stronger, and why?
What distinction does Sita draw between what was in her control and what was not? How does her answer show her dignity?
How is this ending different from the fire ordeal? What might Sita's choice say about her voice at the end of the story?
How might changing the center of the story change what a listener feels about the fire ordeal and Sita's exile?

15.bq: Why do careful readers of the same sacred texts reach different conclusions, and how can a student describe those readings fairly?
std: Evaluate the methods people and institutions have used to promote change.
Analyze the factors and context that shaped people's perspectives in different eras.
Evaluate authors' differing points of view on the same issue by weighing their claims, reasoning and evidence.
Teaching About Religion · expose not impose
Introduce a range of religious views without imposing any particular one.
15.write: Choose one passage (tat tvam asi, Chandogya 6.8.7; or Gita 18.66 or 2.47) and explain how three readers, at least one classical and one modern, have read it. Cite the passage and translation, give each reader's reasoning in terms they would accept, and argue why their readings differ.
rooms: One question, many lenses — the room

ch.t: Shankara, Ramanuja, Madhva
ch.bq: How can three careful commentators read the same sacred words and reach three different accounts of God, the self and the world?
ch.talk: If three expert readers disagree about four words, what does that suggest about reading sacred texts? Is disagreement a failure, or part of the tradition?

l.look: Why might stating the opposing view well make an argument stronger, not weaker? How could you use this method in your own essay?
Why might a very short text like the Brahma Sutras invite more disagreement than a longer one?
In Shankara's image, what is the rope, what is the snake, and what is the lamp? What does the image say about how liberation happens?
Which words in the phrase does Shankara say must be "set aside"? Why is that step needed for his reading to work?
Why might a tradition place its centers at four corners of a land? What does the map suggest about Shankara's aims?
How does this analogy keep both unity and difference? Which Advaita claim does it reject?
Compare this to Shankara's reading. Which word does each thinker treat differently?
Which of these differences would Shankara deny at the highest level? Which would Ramanuja accept?
How can the same sounds support two readings? What else besides grammar would a commentator use to decide?
Explain how each reading fits that school's view of the self and God. Which word in the verse does each reading lean on most?

ch.t: Modern Readers: Reform, Freedom and the West
ch.bq: Why did the Gita and the Upanishads become texts for reform, for freedom struggles and for readers far from India, and why did those readers disagree?
ch.talk: Gandhi called a war poem his mother and a guide to nonviolence. What would a reader need to believe about the poem for that to make sense?
ch.story: A Small Book in a Cell

l.t: Ram Mohan Roy and the Upanishads
l.look: Why might an argument from a community's own texts persuade some people more than an argument from outside? What risks does that approach carry?
Vivekananda died at 39. What does the short time between 1893 and 1902 suggest about how quickly his influence spread?
Which Gita verses could each reader cite? Think of 2.47, 3.8, 3.19 and 18.66.
What role does Gandhi give the Gita in his life? How is this different from reading it as a history or a law book?
Several modern readers turned to the Gita in prison. What might a prisoner find in a book about action, duty and letting go of results?
Who is the "he" who speaks in Emerson's poem? Compare the idea to Gita 2.19. What did Emerson keep, and what did he change?
At each link, what did the reader keep and what did they add? Is the chain one idea passing along, or a new idea at each step?
How does each reader use the words "qualities and actions"? State each position in words its holder would accept.
Pick two readers who were active at nearly the same time. How did their settings differ?

16.bq: How have readers used sacred texts both to uphold and to challenge injustice, and how can we compare scriptures fairly?
std: Analyze key events and contributions through varied perspectives, including those of underrepresented groups.
Evaluate authors' differing points of view on the same issue by weighing their claims, reasoning and evidence.
Integrate information from diverse sources into a coherent understanding, noting where they disagree.
Teaching About Religion · educate not promote or denigrate
Present every tradition fairly, neither advancing nor disparaging religion.
16.write: Choose one theme (duty, nonviolence or devotion, or caste and scripture). Cite two or three passages from this unit (for example Gita 2.47, Matthew 6:3–4, Dhammapada 5, Manusmriti 3.56 and 9.3; name the translation), explain what each says, and describe how its readers have understood it, comparing without ranking.

ch.t: Caste, Gender and the Texts
ch.bq: How have Hindu texts been used to support and to challenge hierarchies of caste and gender, and how have Hindus themselves responded?
ch.talk: Burning a book is a strong symbol. What did it mean to the people at Mahad, and why might other Hindus have seen it differently?

l.look: Why might it matter, in a history essay, whether a writer means varna or jati when they say "caste"? Give an example of a confusion that could result.
How can both verses be in the same book? How might a traditional reader, a reformer and a feminist scholar each explain them?
Which details from the Adi Parva does each version stress? Which version would you use to teach younger students, and why?
What does Basava replace the stone temple with? What does that say about who can worship?
What does Ravidas's city lack? Why would a poet who faced untouchability picture a city this way?
Phule dedicated Gulamgiri to American abolitionists. What does that suggest about how he saw his struggle?
Why might the order of these two events matter? What did each act say, and to whom?
Why might new laws have been needed after the Constitution already abolished untouchability?
What does Maitreyi's question show about what she values? Compare her choice to Nachiketa's in the Katha Upanishad.
Does it change a song's meaning if Mirabai herself did not write it? How might a scholar and a devotee answer differently?

ch.t: The Gita Beside Other Scriptures
ch.bq: What can we learn by reading the Gita beside other scriptures on duty, nonviolence and devotion, without ranking any of them?
ch.talk: Gandhi, Tolstoy and King each read another religion's scripture closely. What might a reader gain from that, and what might they miss?

l.look: Which comparison teaches you more about each text? What does Comparison A lose?
These texts differ greatly in form. How might a short saying collection and a long poem teach differently?
What does each vision answer, and what does it leave unanswered? How is each hero changed by what he sees?

l.t: Action and Its Fruits in the Dhammapada
l.look: What do both passages say about the mind behind an action? What different view of the self stands behind each?

l.t: Role and Rightness in the Analects
l.look: How does this principle compare with the Gita's teaching on svadharma? Is it about roles, or about all people equally?

l.t: Ahimsa in Jain and Buddhist Texts
l.look: How might a nonviolent movement use this verse? Compare it with Gita 2.62–2.63 on anger.
What does each passage say about reward? Who or what, in each text, stands behind the action?
What image does each text use for the divine's care? How does the speaker differ in each (who is speaking to whom)?
In one image the flute cries; in the other it calls. What does that difference suggest about each tradition's picture of longing?

17.t: The Texts in Life, and Capstone
17.bq: How do Hindu texts live in performance and community today, and how can a student make a careful argument about what a passage means to its readers?
std: Cite strong textual evidence, linking details to an understanding of the text as a whole.
Write arguments with precise claims, fairly developed counterclaims and well-chosen evidence.
Draw evidence from informational texts to support analysis, reflection and research.
Teaching About Religion · academic not devotional
Study religion as an academic subject that describes beliefs and practices without leading worship.
17.write: Capstone: choose one passage (a Gita verse, an Upanishad dialogue, a Rig Veda hymn or an epic episode). Cite it exactly with its translation, set its context, present three readings (a classical commentator, a modern reader and a scholar), and argue why they differ, answering one counterargument.
rooms: World Religions capstone — the sources speak

ch.t: Texts in Performance, Art and Diaspora
ch.bq: How do Hindu texts live beyond the page, in drama, dance, stone, comics, television and diaspora communities, and who gets to speak for them?
ch.talk: What does Meera learn from dancing Sita's scene that she might not learn from reading it? What might a reader learn that a dancer might not?

l.look: Why might a performance that lasts a month teach a story differently from a two-hour play?
How can a scene be understood without spoken words? What skills does the audience need?
The stories moved across the sea over centuries. What does this suggest about how the epics traveled?
Why might a comic for children choose one version? What might be gained, and what might be lost?
Why might a series from 1987 still draw viewers in 2020? What does that say about the story or the moment?
Why might diaspora temples bring many shrines together? How might that change what children learn about the texts?
If a school held a Diwali assembly, how could it present the festival fairly to families who tell different stories?
For each case, how might different Hindu Americans respond? What questions would help decide whether a use shows appreciation or appropriation?
List the words in Textbook A that a Hindu student might find unfair. What does Textbook B do differently? Is anything still missing?

ch.t: Capstone: A Passage, Its Readers and Your Argument
ch.bq: What does one passage mean to its readers, why do they read it differently, and how can you make a careful argument about it?
ch.talk: Jalen notices that all three readers begin with the same word. Why might a single word be the place where readings split apart?

l.look: Write a too-big, better and just-right question for a passage you might choose.
Identify the four parts of this citation: text, location, translator, edition and year. Why does each part matter?
How would you state both dates in one fair sentence that names who holds each?
Fill in a row for a scholar of religion. What would a scholar focus on that the others do not?
Rewrite another list sentence from this course as an analysis sentence with "because."
Write one claim a reader might make about this line, then one sentence of explanation connecting the line to that claim.
Rewrite each sentence so the belief is attributed to a text, tradition or reader. Example: "Gita 2.20 says the self never dies."
Which step will take you longest to prepare, even if it is short to present? Why?
